citations.quote: Let $\mathbb Z[t]$ be the polynomial ring over the integers ([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]], [[thm-polynomial-ring-is-a-commutative-ring]]) and let $$S=\{t^k:k\ge0\}.$$ The set $S$ is multiplicative, and the **Laurent polynomial ring** is the principal localisation $$\Lambda_1:=\mathbb Z[t]_S=S^{-1}\mathbb Z[t]$$ ([[def-principal-localisation]], [[def-multiplicative-subset-and-loc

Let $K$ be a field and let $v$ be a discrete valuation on $K$ ([[def-discrete-valuation]]). Its **valuation ring** is $$ V_v:=\{x\in K:v(x)\ge 0\}. $$ This is a valuation ring in the sense of [[def-valuation-ring]]. A **discrete valuation ring** (DVR) is a subring $V\subseteq K$ of the form $V=V_v$ for some discrete valuation $v$ on $K$.

Let $R$ be a ring ([[def-ring]]) with identity $1_R$ and zero $0_R$. For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ let $n \cdot 1_R$ be the additive natural power of $1_R$ in the abelian group $(R,+,0_R)$ ([[def-group-power]], [[def-group]]): thus $0 \cdot 1_R = 0_R$ and $\sigma(n)\cdot 1_R = n \cdot 1_R + 1_R$.

derivations.claim: Reduction to $N$ and to $A/B$. Since $Bt^v$ is a unit of $F[t,t^{-1}]$ with inverse $B^{-1}t^{-v}$ by [F1], the identity $At^u-Bt^v=Bt^v\bigl((A/B)t^N-1\bigr)$ and [F2] give $v_1(At^u-Bt^v)=v_1\bigl((A/B)t^N-1\bigr)$; moreover if $N<0$ then $t^{N}-1=-t^{N}(t^{-N}-1)$ with $-t^{N}$ a unit, so $v_1(t^{N}-1)=v_1(t^{|N|}-1)$ by [F1] and [F2]. [F1, F2]

The case $A=B$, $N=0$. Then $f=At^u-Bt^v=At^u-At^u=0$ by [F1], the zero element of $F[t,t^{-1}]$; since $(t-1)^n\mid0$ for every $n$, the set in the definition of $v_1$ is unbounded and no finite value is assigned. [F1]

The case $A\ne B$. Evaluating the Laurent polynomial $(A/B)t^N-1$ at $t=1$ gives $A/B-1\ne0$, so the factor $t-1$ cannot divide $(A/B)t^N-1$: a product containing $t-1$ would evaluate to $0$ under the ring homomorphism $f\mapsto f(1)$ with $1\mapsto1$. Hence $v_1((A/B)t^N-1)=0$ by [F2], and the reduction of step 1.1 gives $v_1(f)=0$. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

The case $A=B$, $\operatorname{char}F=0$, $N\ne0$. Here $f=A(t^u-t^v)=At^v(t^N-1)$ with $At^v$ a unit, so by step 1.1 the valuation equals $v_1(t^{|N|}-1)$, while $t^{|N|}-1=(t-1)(1+t+\cdots+t^{|N|-1})$ with second factor evaluating at $t=1$ to $|N|\cdot1_F\ne0$ by [F3] and therefore of valuation $0$ by [F2]; the valuation is additive on this factorisation of the nonzero polynomial $t^{|N|}-1$, so $v_1(f)=1$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

The case $A=B$, $\operatorname{char}F=p>0$, $N
e0$. Write $|N|=p^rm$ with $r\ge0$ and $p
mid m$. In characteristic $p$ the identity $(x-1)^{p^r}=x^{p^r}-1$ follows by iterating $(x-1)^p=x^p-1$ (the intermediate binomial coefficients $ inom{p}{i}$, $1\le i\le p-1$, are multiples of $p$); applying it to $x=t^m$ gives $t^{|N|}-1=(t^m-1)^{p^r}=(t-1)^{p^r}(1+t+\cdots+t^{m-1})^{p^r}$. The second factor evaluates at $t=1$ to $m^{p^r}\cdot1_F$, which is nonzero because $m\cdot1_F
e0$ by [F3]; it thus has valuation $0$ by [F2], so $v_1(t^{|N|}-1)=p^r$, and step 1.1 gives $v_1(f)=p^r=p^{v_p(|N|)}$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

citations.quote: A **free abelian group on a set $X$** is an abelian group $A(X)$ together with a map $i:X\to A(X)$ such that, for every abelian group $B$ and every function $u:X\to B$, there is a unique group homomorphism $\widehat u:A(X)\to B$ satisfying $$\widehat u\circ i=u.$$
On the set $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ of pairs of natural numbers, define $$(a,b) \sim (c,d) \iff a + d = b + c.$$ This is an equivalence relation ([[lem-int-equivalence]]).

Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a combinatorial class. An object of $\operatorname{MSET}(\mathcal{A})$ is a finitely supported multiplicity function $$m : \mathcal{A} \to \mathbb{N},$$ whose value $m(a)$ records how many copies of $a$ occur. Its size is $$|m| := \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}} m(a)|a|,$$ which is a finite sum because the support of $m$ is finite.

derivations.claim: Elementary cases and well-definedness. The empty multiset is ultra-tight (its images under zero-exchange sequences are empty, hence tight) and satisfies the displayed condition with $s=0$; for $r=1$ one has $L_1=\mathbb Z/\mathbb Z\cdot1=0$ by [F1], so $x_1-x_1=0$ for every occurrence, every finite multiset is tight, and no zero exchange exists because its defining equation reads $0-0=2$; thus every finite multiset in $L_1$ is ultra-tight and satisfies the condition with $s=0$. By [F1] the differences $x_k-x_l$ do not change when representatives are shifted by a multiple of $(1,\dots,1)$, so tightness and the zero-exchange steps are well defined on classes; a zero-exchange sequence may therefore be computed with any representatives. [F1, F2]

The reverse implication. Assume $s\in\mathbb Z^r$ satisfies the displayed condition. Replacing each occurrence $x\in X$ by $x-s$ (a bijection of $L_r$ by [F1]) we may assume $x_k-x_l\le1$ for all $x,k,l$; applying this to the pair $(l,k)$ gives $x_l-x_k\le1$, so $|x_k-x_l|\le1$ for all $x,k,l$. We prove by induction on the length of a zero-exchange sequence that every such multiset is tight, and suppress the shift by $s$ from the notation. Suppose the next exchange acts on $x,y\in X$ in coordinates $k,l$, so $(x_k-x_l)-(y_k-y_l)=2$. Since $x_k-x_l,y_k-y_l\in[-1,1]$, this forces $x_k-x_l=1$ and $y_k-y_l=-1$; writing $x'=x-e_k+e_l$ and $y'=y+e_k-e_l$, the coordinate differences of $x'$ are $x'_k-x'_l=-1$, and for $p\notin\{k,l\}$ we have $x'_k-x'_p=x_k-1-x_p\in[-1,1]$, $x'_p-x'_k=x_p-x_k+1\in[-1,1]$, $x'_l-x'_p=x_k-x_p\in[-1,1]$ and $x'_p-x'_l=x_p-x_l-1\in[-1,1]$, using $x_k=x_l+1$ and $|x_p-x_q|\le1$; the same computation with $y$ in place of $x$ and $y_l=y_k+1$ shows the same for $y'$. All other occurrences are unchanged and already have all coordinate differences in $[-1,1]$. Hence in every reachable multiset all coordinate differences lie in $[-1,1]$, and for any two occurrences $z,w$ of that multiset $(z_k-z_l)-(w_k-w_l)\le1-(-1)=2$: every reachable multiset is tight, so $X$ is ultra-tight. [F1, algebra]

Setup for the forward implication. Conversely assume $X$ ultra-tight; we prove by induction on $r$ that potentials $s\in\mathbb Z^r$ exist satisfying the displayed condition. The case $r=1$ is in step 1.1. Let $r\ge2$ and assume the result for $r-1$. Let $\pi\colon L_r\to L_{r-1}$ forget the last coordinate; every zero exchange in $\pi(X)$ in coordinates $k,l\le r-1$ lifts to the zero exchange in $X$ with the same coordinates and the same labelled occurrences, because the defining difference of the pair is unchanged; hence every zero-exchange sequence in $\pi(X)$ is the projection of one in $X$ and ends tight. So $\pi(X)$ is ultra-tight, and by induction there are integers $s_1,\dots,s_{r-1}$ with $x_k-x_l\le s_k-s_l+1$ for all $x\in X$ and $k,l\le r-1$; applying this to $(l,k)$ gives, with $a_{kl}:=s_k-s_l$, $\bigl|(x_k-x_l)-a_{kl}\bigr|\le1\qquad(k,l\le r-1).$ It remains to extend the potentials to the last coordinate: we must choose $s_r$ so that $|(x_k-x_r)-a_{kr}|\le1$ for all $x\in X$ and all $k\le r-1$, where now $a_{kr}=s_k-s_r$. It is enough to do this in the descending sequence of stages described below: at stage $t=r-1,\dots,1$ one adds the bounds for the single pair $(t,r)$ while keeping all bounds already proved for pairs with both entries $\le r-1$ or both entries $\ge t+1$. [F1, F2]

The stage $t=r-1$. Since $X$ is ultra-tight, the empty sequence shows that $X$ itself is tight; hence for all $x,y\in X$, $(x_{r-1}-x_r)-(y_{r-1}-y_r)\le2$ and, exchanging $x$ and $y$, $\ge-2$. The integers $x_{r-1}-x_r$ therefore have range at most $2$, so (choosing the integer midpoint) some integer $m$ satisfies $|(x_{r-1}-x_r)-m|\le1$ for all $x\in X$; choosing $s_r:=s_{r-1}-m$ gives $a_{r-1,r}=m$ and hence the pair-$(r-1,r)$ bound, while all bounds of step 2.1 with $k,l\le r-1$ are unchanged. [F2, step 2.1, algebra]

Reduction to the exceptional case. Fix $t\le r-1$ and suppose the bounds $|(x_k-x_l)-a_{kl}|\le1$ are known for all $x\in X$ whenever $k,l\le r-1$ or $k,l\ge t+1$ (for $t=r-1$ this is step 3.1 together with step 2.1). We show that the bounds also hold for all pairs with $k,l\ge t$; as observed in step 2.1, the only new pair to control is $(t,r)$. If already $|(x_t-x_r)-a_{tr}|\le1$ for all $x$, there is nothing to prove. Otherwise some $x\in X$ has $x_t-x_r\ge a_{tr}+2$ or $x_t-x_r\le a_{tr}-2$; replacing every occurrence $x$ by $-x$ and every $s_k$ by $-s_k$ (which preserves ultra-tightness and all current bounds by [F1]) we may assume the first case, so that for this $x$, $x_t-x_r\ge a_{tr}+2 .$ [step 3.1, given]

Consequences of the choice of $x$, and the sandwich. For every $u\in\{t+1,\dots,r-1\}$ the known bounds give $x_t-x_u\le a_{tu}+1$ and $x_u-x_r\le a_{ur}+1$, so $x_t-x_r=(x_t-x_u)+(x_u-x_r)\le a_{tu}+a_{ur}+2=a_{tr}+2$; together with the choice of $x$ this forces equality throughout: $x_t-x_u=a_{tu}+1,\qquad x_u-x_r=a_{ur}+1\qquad(t<u<r).$ Tightness of $X$ applied to the pair $x,y$, in both orders, gives $(x_t-x_r)-(y_t-y_r)\le2$ and $\ge-2$, i.e. with $x_t-x_r=a_{tr}+2$, $a_{tr}\le y_t-y_r\le a_{tr}+2\qquad\text{for every }y\in X .$ [step 4.1, algebra]

The graph, the basic lower bound, and the case of no path. Draw a directed graph $G$ on $\{1,\dots,r\}$ with an arrow $k\to l$ if and only if some $y\in X$ satisfies $y_k-y_l=a_{kl}-1$. First we note that $x_k-x_r\ge a_{kr}+1\qquad\text{for every }k<r:$ for $k=u\ge t+1$ this is the equality $x_u-x_r=a_{ur}+1$ of step 5.1, for $k=t$ it follows from $x_t-x_r\ge a_{tr}+2$, and for $k<t$ it follows from $x_k-x_r=(x_k-x_t)+(x_t-x_r)\ge (a_{kt}-1)+(a_{tr}+2)=a_{kr}+1$ using the known bound for the pair $(k,t)$ with $k,t\le r-1$. Suppose first that $G$ contains no directed path from $t$ to $r$. Let $T$ be the set of vertices reachable from $t$ (so $t\in T$, $r\notin T$) and let $R$ be its complement; there is no arrow from $T$ to $R$, since such an arrow would put its target in $T$. Define new potentials $\hat s_k:=s_k+1$ for $k\in T$ and $\hat s_k:=s_k$ for $k\in R$, and set $\hat a_{kl}:=\hat s_k-\hat s_l$. Then $\hat a_{tr}=a_{tr}+1,\qquad \hat a_{kl}\in\{a_{kl}-1,a_{kl},a_{kl}+1\},$ and $\hat a_{kl}=a_{kl}-1$ occurs exactly for $k\in R$, $l\in T$. The new $(t,r)$ bound follows from the sandwich of step 5.1: $\hat a_{tr}-1=a_{tr}\le y_t-y_r\le a_{tr}+2=\hat a_{tr}+1$ for all $y\in X$. For any other pair the bound is immediate if $\hat a_{kl}\ge a_{kl}$, since the old upper bound $y_k-y_l\le a_{kl}+1\le\hat a_{kl}+1$ survives. If $\hat a_{kl}=a_{kl}-1$, then $k\in R$, $l\in T$; the absence of an arrow from $T$ to $R$ says no $y$ has $y_l-y_k=a_{lk}-1$, so the old lower bound $y_l-y_k\ge a_{lk}-1$ improves to $y_l-y_k\ge a_{lk}$ for all $y$, i.e. $y_k-y_l\le -a_{lk}=a_{kl}=\hat a_{kl}+1$. Thus the bounds hold for all pairs with both entries in $\{t,\dots,r\}$, as required, and stage $t$ is complete in the no-path case. [step 5.1, algebra]

The case of a path: the witnesses. Now suppose $G$ contains a directed path from $t$ to $r$, and let $t=k_1\to k_2\to\cdots\to k_h=r$ be one of minimal length (so $k_1,\dots,k_h$ are pairwise distinct by [F2]). For each $m=1,\dots,h-1$ choose an occurrence $y_m\in X$ witnessing the arrow $k_m\to k_{m+1}$, i.e. $y_{m,k_m}-y_{m,k_{m+1}}=a_{k_mk_{m+1}}-1$, and put $x^{(m)}:=x-e_{k_{m+1}}+e_r\qquad(1\le m<h),$ so that $x^{(h-1)}=x$ because $k_h=r$. We shall prove by downward induction on $m$ that there is a multiset $Y_m\equiv X$ (in the equivalence relation generated by zero exchanges) containing $y_1,\dots,y_m$ and $x^{(m)}$, and that the following two statements hold: $B_m:\quad (x^{(m)}_{k_m}-x^{(m)}_{k_{m+1}})-(y_{m,k_m}-y_{m,k_{m+1}})=2, \qquad C_m:\quad x_{k_m}-x_r=a_{k_m r}+1 .$ Reading $C_1$ together with step 4.1 (which gives $x_{k_1}-x_r=x_t-x_r\ge a_{tr}+2$) will then contradict the choice of $x$; the contradiction is completed below. We record $B_{h-1}$ and $C_{h-1}$: by the basic lower bound of step 6.1, $(x_{k_{h-1}}-x_r)-(y_{h-1,k_{h-1}}-y_{h-1,r})\ge(a_{k_{h-1}r}+1)-(a_{k_{h-1}r}-1)=2$, while tightness of $Y_{h-1}:=X$ gives $\le2$; hence equality holds, which is $B_{h-1}$, and then $C_{h-1}$ follows because $y_{h-1,k_{h-1}}-y_{h-1,r}=a_{k_{h-1}r}-1$ and $(x_{k_{h-1}}-x_r)-(y_{h-1,k_{h-1}}-y_{h-1,r})=2$. [step 6.1, given]

The induction step constructing $Y_m$. Let $m\le h-2$ and assume $A_{m+1}$ and $B_{m+1}$, where $A_{m+1}$ says that $Y_{m+1}\equiv X$ contains $y_1,\dots,y_{m+1}$ and $x^{(m+1)}$. Form $Y_m$ from $Y_{m+1}$ by removing the occurrences $x^{(m+1)}$ and $y_{m+1}$ and adding the occurrences $x^{(m)}$ and $y_{m+1}+e_{k_{m+1}}-e_{k_{m+2}}$. By $B_{m+1}$ the pair $\bigl(x^{(m+1)},y_{m+1}\bigr)$ has difference exactly $2$ in coordinates $(k_{m+1},k_{m+2})$, so this is a zero exchange; hence $Y_m\equiv Y_{m+1}\equiv X$ by $A_{m+1}$, and $Y_m$ contains $y_1,\dots,y_m$ and $x^{(m)}$. Thus $A_m$ holds. [step 7.1, algebra]

The induction step forcing $B_m$ and $C_m$, and the contradiction. Let $m\le h-2$ and assume $A_m$ and $C_{m+1}$. Since $k_1,\dots,k_h$ are pairwise distinct and only $k_h$ equals $r$, the $r$-th coordinate of $e_r$ vanishes in positions $k_m$ and $k_{m+1}$, so $x^{(m)}_{k_m}-x^{(m)}_{k_{m+1}} =(x_{k_m}-x_r)-(x_{k_{m+1}}-x_r)+1 \ge (a_{k_m r}+1)-(a_{k_{m+1}r}+1)+1 =a_{k_mk_{m+1}}+1 =y_{m,k_m}-y_{m,k_{m+1}}+2,$ where the inequality uses the basic lower bound of step 6.1 for $k_m$ and statement $C_{m+1}$ for $k_{m+1}$. Since $Y_m$ is tight (it lies in the class of the ultra-tight $X$), the reverse inequality holds and we have equality, which is $B_m$; reading the equality back through the displayed chain gives $x_{k_m}-x_r=a_{k_m r}+1$, which is $C_m$. Downward induction on $m$ now gives $C_1$, i.e. $x_{k_1}-x_r=x_t-x_r=a_{tr}+1$, contradicting $x_t-x_r\ge a_{tr}+2$ from the choice of $x$ in step 4.1. Hence the exceptional case cannot occur: with the current potentials the pair $(t,r)$ is already bounded, so stage $t$ is complete in the path case as well. [step 7.1, step 8.1, algebra]

Completion of the induction. Stages $t=r-1,r-2,\dots,1$ have now been treated: each stage either leaves the potentials unchanged, or (in the no-path case of step 6.1) replaces them by potentials for which the new bound holds, while all bounds proved earlier are preserved (the modification changes $s_k-s_l$ by at most $1$ in the necessary direction, and the argument of step 6.1 checks both the improved and the unchanged pairs). After stage $1$ the bounds hold for all pairs $k,l$ with $k,l\le r-1$ or $k,l\ge1$, i.e. for all $k,l\in\{1,\dots,r\}$. This proves the forward implication for $r$, and with the base case $r=1$ of step 1.1 and the induction scheme of step 2.1, the forward implication for all $r\ge1$. Combined with the reverse implication of step 1.2, an ultra-tight multiset is exactly one admitting column potentials $s$, including the empty multiset and the case $r=1$. [step 1.1, step 6.1, step 9.1] ∎

citations.quote:
Let $K$ be a field and let $v$ be a discrete valuation on $K$
([[def-discrete-valuation]]). Its **valuation ring** is
$$ V_v:=\{x\in K:v(x)\ge 0\}. $$
This is a valuation ring in the sense of [[def-valuation-ring]].

A **discrete valuation ring** (DVR) is a subring $V\subseteq K$ of the form
$V=V_v$ for some discrete valuation $v$ on $K$. Because $v$ is surjective,
there is an element of value $1$, so $V$ has a nonunit and is therefore not a
field.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

Let $R$ be a ring. A **left $R$-module** is an abelian group $(M,+,0_M)$ with a
scalar action $R\times M\to M$, $(r,m)\mapsto rm$, satisfying

$$r(m+n)=rm+rn,\quad (r+s)m=rm+sm,\quad (rs)m=r(sm),\quad 1_Rm=m.$$

A **right $R$-module** has an action $M\times R\to M$, $(m,r)\mapsto mr$, with
the analogous right-handed axioms. Unless “right” is stated, **module** means a
unital left module.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra and $M$ a finite-dimensional left
$A$-module.

- Its **radical** is
  $$   \operatorname{rad}(M)=J(A)M,   $$
  equivalently the intersection of the maximal submodules, by
  [[thm-module-radical-is-jacobson-radical-times-the-module]].

- Its **socle** $\operatorname{Soc}(M)$ is the sum of all simple submodules, as
  in [[def-socle-of-a-module]].

- Its **head** or **top** is the quotient
  $$   \operatorname{hd}(M):=M/\operatorname{rad}(M),   $$
  formed using [[def-quotient-module]].

- Its **Loewy series** is the descending radical filtration
  $$   M\supseteq \operatorname{rad}(M)\supseteq \operatorname{rad}^2(M)\supseteq\cdots   $$
  together with the corresponding semisimple layers
  $\operatorname{rad}^i(M)/\operatorname{rad}^{i+1}(M)$.

The simple subquotients appearing in the Loewy layers are simple in the sense
of [[def-simple-module]].

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and $A$ a unital $R$-algebra
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) that is free as an $R$-module on a
finite set $C=\{c^{\lambda}_{st}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ s,t\in T(\lambda)\}$,
where $(\Lambda,\unrhd)$ is a finite poset ([[def-partial-order]]; its strict
order is written $\rhd$) and each $T(\lambda)$ is a finite set. For
$\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ be the $R$-submodule of $A$ spanned
by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$.

Then $(C,\Lambda)$ is a **cellular basis** of $A$, and $A$ is a **cellular
algebra**, if:

(i) the $R$-linear map $i:A\to A$ with $i(c^{\lambda}_{st})=c^{\lambda}_{ts}$
for all $\lambda,s,t$ is an algebra anti-automorphism of $A$, i.e. $i(ab)=i(b)i(a)$
and $i(1)=1$ (equivalently $i$ is an isomorphism of $A$ with the opposite
algebra; the displayed formula forces $i^2=\mathrm{id}$); and

(ii) for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$, every $t\in T(\lambda)$ and every $a\in A$
there exist $r_v\in R$ ($v\in T(\lambda)$) with
$$c^{\lambda}_{st}\,a\equiv\sum_{v\in T(\lambda)}r_v\,c^{\lambda}_{sv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}.$$

**Cell modules.** For $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $C^{\lambda}$ be the free
$R$-module with basis $\{c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_{tt}:t\in T(\lambda)\}$;
condition (ii) makes $C^{\lambda}$ a right $A$-module by
$c^{\lambda}_t a:=\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_v$ when
$c^{\lambda}_{tt}a\equiv\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_{tv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$, and
it makes $C^{\lambda}$ a left $A$-module via $i$, the left action being
$a\cdot c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_t\,i(a)$. Both actions are well defined on
the freely spanning basis elements by (ii): the coefficients $r_v$ are unique
because $C$ is an $R$-basis of $A$ and the quotient by $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ kills
exactly the basis elements indexed by strictly larger labels, while applying
the anti-automorphism (i) to (ii) gives the same triangularity for left
multiplication. The module $C^{\lambda}$ is the **(right) cell module** of
$\lambda$, and
$$A^{\unrhd\lambda}/A^{\rhd\lambda}\cong C^{\lambda}\otimes_R C^{\lambda}$$
via $c^{\lambda}_{st}+A^{\rhd\lambda}\mapsto c^{\lambda}_s\otimes c^{\lambda}_t$,
where $A^{\unrhd\lambda}$ is spanned by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with
$\mu\unrhd\lambda$. A cellular algebra may have several cellular bases.

derivations.claim: The rank-zero case. If $n=0$, then $M=0$ and $M^*=0$, the pairing is generically nondegenerate on the zero space, and $M(s)=M_F^s=0$ for every $s$. The empty Gram determinant is defined here by the empty Leibniz product to be $1$, whose valuation is $0$; the empty sum of elementary-divisor exponents is $0$. Thus the Gram valuation identity is $0=0$, the radical and stability assertions hold, and the conditional nonzero-cellular-form assertion has no rank-zero instance. For the remaining steps assume $n\ge1$.

Smith reduction of the form. View $b$ as the $O$-linear map $\varphi\colon M\to M^*$, $\varphi(x)=b(x,-)$, with matrix $G^{\mathsf T}$ in column coordinates by [F2]; nondegeneracy over $\operatorname{Frac}(O)$ gives $\det G\ne0$, so $\varphi$ has full rank. Choose a nonzero matrix entry of $\varphi$ of least valuation $\nu_\pi$ and move it to position $(1,1)$ by permuting the bases, then multiply its row by a unit of $O$ to make it $\pi^{a_1}$; every entry of the matrix is divisible by $\pi^{a_1}$ by minimality (including zero entries). Subtracting suitable $O$-multiples of the first row from the other rows and of the first column from the other columns (all coefficients in $O$, all operations unimodular by [F1]) kills the first row and column outside position $(1,1)$, leaving a smaller matrix over $O$. Iterating over the remaining rows and columns produces bases $u_1,\dots,u_n$ of $M$ and $v_1,\dots,v_n$ of $M^*$ with $\varphi(u_j)=\pi^{a_j}v_j$ and $0\le a_1\le\dots\le a_n$.

Reduction of the radical. For $\bar x\in M_F$ one has $b_F(\bar x,M_F)=0$ if and only if $b(x,M)\subseteq\pi O$, i.e. $x\in M(1)$; hence $\operatorname{rad}(b_F)=(M(1)+\pi M)/\pi M=M_F^1$ by [F3], the containment $\pi M\subseteq M(1)$ being immediate from $b(\pi x,M)\subseteq\pi O$.

Submodule stability. Let $a\in A$ and $x\in M(s)$; by the hypothesis $b(ax,y)=b(x,a^*y)\in\pi^sO$ for every $y\in M$, since $a^*y\in M$. Hence $ax\in M(s)$ and $M(s)$ is an $A$-submodule; consequently $M_F^s=(M(s)+\pi M)/\pi M$ is an $A$-submodule of $M_F$, the $\pi M$-cosets of $M(s)$ being stable because $\pi M$ is stable.

The cellular standard module. Assume $M_F$ is a cellular standard module with nonzero cellular form, and let $N\subseteq M_F$ be a proper submodule. If some $w\in N$ lies outside $\operatorname{rad}(b_F)$, choose a label $v$ with $b_F(v,w)\ne0$; by the rank-one action [F4] every basis vector $u$ equals $b_F(v,w)^{-1}$ times the image of $w$ under the cell element of the pair $(u,v)$, so $u\in N$ for every basis label $u$ and $N=M_F$, a contradiction. Thus every proper submodule is contained in $\operatorname{rad}(b_F)$, which is proper because the form is nonzero, and the same rank-one argument shows that the quotient $M_F/\operatorname{rad}(b_F)$ is simple (it has no nonzero proper submodule). Hence $\operatorname{rad}(b_F)$ is the unique maximal submodule of $M_F$, i.e. its module radical by [F3].

The filtration in the Smith bases. In the bases of step 1.2 one computes for $s\ge0$ that $b(u_j,M)=\pi^{a_j}O$, so $M(s)=\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n}\pi^{\max(0,s-a_j)}Ou_j,\qquad \dim_FM_F^s=\#\{j:a_j\ge s\}.$ In particular $M(0)=M$, so $M_F^0=M/\pi M$; the reduced filtration terminates because every summand of $M(s)$ is contained in $\pi M$ for $s>\max_ja_j$, so $M_F^s=0$; and each $M_F^s$ is a subspace of the finite-dimensional $F$-space $M_F$.

The Gram valuation identity. By the matrix form of step 1.2, the determinant of $G$ equals that of $G^{\mathsf T}$ and hence $\det(\pi^{a_j}\delta_{jk})$ times a unit, since both change-of-basis matrices are invertible over $O$; hence, using additivity of $\nu_\pi$ by [F1], $\nu_\pi(\det G)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_j =\sum_{s>0}\#\{j:a_j\ge s\} =\sum_{s>0}\dim_FM_F^s,$ the middle equality counting each $a_j$ as the number of positive integers $s\le a_j$.

Conclusion. The rank-zero argument of step 1.1 and steps 1.3–1.5 and 2.1–3.1 establish all four assertions of the Statement: the identification of $M_F^0$ and $M_F^1=\operatorname{rad}(b_F)$, the termination together with the exact identity $\sum_{s>0}\dim_FM_F^s=\nu_\pi(\det G)$, the submodule stability under an anti-involution action, and the equality of $\operatorname{rad}(b_F)$ with the module radical in the cellular standard case. The Smith reduction of step 1.2 is valid over any discrete valuation ring, including residue characteristic $2$, because it uses independent domain and codomain bases and no symmetric diagonalization.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge0$ and $\ell\ge1$, and let $z,U_1,\dots,U_\ell$
be units of $R$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). The **arbitrary-level
cyclotomic Hecke algebra** $H_n=H_n(R;z;U_1,\dots,U_\ell)$ is the $R$-algebra
presented by invertible commuting elements $X_1,\dots,X_n$ and generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ subject to the relations
$$(T_i-z)(T_i+1)=0,\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1},\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(|i-j|>1),$$
$$T_iX_iT_i=zX_{i+1},\qquad X_jT_i=T_iX_j\quad(j\notin\{i,i+1\}),\qquad \prod_{a=1}^{\ell}(X_1-U_a)=0 .$$
For $n=0$ set $H_0=R$. The **grading variable** of this page is $v$, not the
unit $z$: the two are identified only where a statement says so explicitly.

**Multipartitions and Murphy data.** An $\ell$-**multipartition** of $n$ is an
ordered tuple $\lambda=(\lambda^{(1)},\dots,\lambda^{(\ell)})$ of partitions
with $\sum_{b}|\lambda^{(b)}|=n$ ([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]).
Multipartitions are partially ordered by dominance, $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ meaning
that $\sum_{b\le k}|\lambda^{(b)}|+\sum_{j\le m}\lambda^{(k)}_j\ge
\sum_{b\le k}|\mu^{(b)}|+\sum_{j\le m}\mu^{(k)}_j$ for all $k,m$. Fill the
diagram $t^\lambda$ with $1,\dots,n$ in component order, then row order, then
column order. Put $a_k:=\sum_{b<k}|\lambda^{(b)}|$,
$u_\lambda:=\prod_{k=1}^{\ell}\prod_{j\le a_k}(X_j-U_k)$,
$x_\lambda:=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}T_w$, and $m_\lambda:=x_\lambda u_\lambda$,
where $S_\lambda$ is the row subgroup: the subgroup of $S_n$ stabilizing the
rows of $t^\lambda$
([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]],
[[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Write $M_\lambda:=m_\lambda H_n$ for
the right $H_n$-submodule generated by $m_\lambda$
([[def-left-and-right-modules]]). The **presentation involution** $*$ of $H_n$
fixes every $X_j$ and every $T_i$ and reverses products. For standard
tableaux $s,t$ of shape $\lambda$ put $m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^{*}m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$,
where $d(s)$ is the permutation determined by $t^\lambda d(s)=s$.
Denote by $H^{>\lambda}$ the span of the higher Murphy shapes once their
basis and cell law is established by
[[thm-arbitrary-level-cyclotomic-hecke-murphy-basis-is-cellular]], and by
$S_\lambda$ the right cell (**Specht**) module with basis $m_t$ and the
action given by that cell law; its cellular form defines
$D_\lambda:=S_\lambda/\operatorname{rad}S_\lambda$, which may vanish.

**Types.** The types used below are **exactly** all $\ell$-multipartitions of
$n$, including tuples with empty components — not all multicompositions. A
**semistandard tableau** $S$ has entries the labels $(i,k)$ (row $i$ in
component $k$) ordered by component first and then by row, weakly increasing
along rows, strictly increasing down columns, and a label of component $a$
may occur only in physical component $b\le a$
([[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]]); the **type** of $S$ is the
multipartition counting each label with the multiplicity of the corresponding
row. For standard $s$ let $\mu(s)$ be the tableau obtained from $s$ by
replacing each entry by its row-and-component in $t^{\mu}$. Put
$$m_{(S,t)}:=\sum_{s:\,\mu(s)=S}m_{st},\qquad m_{(S,T)}:=\sum_{s,t:\,\mu(s)=S,\ \nu(t)=T}m_{st}.$$
Let
$$M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda\ \text{multipartition of}\ n}M_\lambda,\qquad C_n:=\operatorname{End}_{H_n}(M),$$
with ordinary composition ([[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]). For
$S,T$ of shape $\lambda$ and types $\mu,\nu$, the map $\varphi_{ST}$ — once
justified by [[lem-cyclotomic-semistandard-sums-give-schur-endomorphism-basis]] —
sends $m_\alpha h$ to $\delta_{\alpha,\nu}m_{(S,T)}h$. Its right cell module
$\Delta_\lambda$ has basis $v_T$ over the semistandard $T$ of multipartition
types, with contravariant cell form and quotient $L_\lambda$. Let $T^\lambda$
be the unique tableau of shape and type $\lambda$, and let $e_\lambda$ be the
identity projection onto $M_\lambda$. Put $\omega:=(\varnothing,\dots,\varnothing,(1^n))$
and $e:=e_\omega$; then $m_\omega=1$, so $M_\omega=H_n$, and $H_n$ is an
actual direct summand of $M$. The weight projections used by the Jantzen
theory below are the $e_\nu$ with $\nu$ a multipartition. Write
$K_{(\lambda,\nu)}:=\#\operatorname{SStd}_\nu(\lambda)$ for the number of
semistandard tableaux of shape $\lambda$ and type $\nu$.

**Boundary of the definition.** All asserted module, form and map laws are
discharged by the linked local suppliers
[[thm-arbitrary-level-cyclotomic-hecke-murphy-basis-is-cellular]],
[[lem-cyclotomic-semistandard-sums-give-schur-endomorphism-basis]] and
[[thm-cyclotomic-schur-standards-and-schur-functor-control-block-linkage]];
the definition itself claims no proof of them and no primitive
residue-content classification. No choice principle is used: only finite
bases, finite subgroup and coset decompositions, finite filtrations and
explicit polynomial identities occur.

In the generic type-A Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with
generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, the quadratic relations
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations, and with
$T_w$ the product of the $T_i$ along a reduced word for $w\in S_n$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]):

1. $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$; in particular $H_v(n)$ is
free of rank $n!$ over $A$;
2. for every $w\in S_n$ and every $1\le i\le n-1$,
$$T_wT_i=T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad T_wT_i=(v-1)T_w+v\,T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1,$$
where $\ell$ is the inversion length of $S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]); consequently the rule rewrites
every monomial in the generators as an $A$-linear combination of the $T_w$.

No choice principle is used.

For $n\ge2$, the symmetric group $S_n$ has the presentation

$$S_n=\langle s_1,\dots,s_{n-1}\mid s_i^2=1,\ s_is_{i+1}s_i=s_{i+1}s_is_{i+1},\ s_is_j=s_js_i\ (|i-j|>1)\rangle,$$

where, after relabelling the underlying set $n=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ as
$\{1,\ldots,n\}$, $s_i$ corresponds to the adjacent transposition
$(i\ i+1)$. For
$n=0,1$, the trivial group has the empty presentation.

derivations.claim: Ordered spanning without localization. For every $f\in P$ the presentation relations give $T_if=s_i(f)T_i+c_{i,i+1}(f-s_i(f))$, where $c_{i,i+1}=(z-1)X_{i+1}/(X_{i+1}-X_i)$. The correction is in $P$: $f-s_i(f)$ is divisible by $X_{i+1}-X_i$, first for ordinary monomials by the difference-of-powers identity, and then for Laurent monomials after multiplying by a symmetric Laurent monomial unit. For $f=X_i$ this is the Bernstein relation, for $f=X_{i+1}$ it is its conjugate using the quadratic relation, and the general formula follows by addition and the product rule $f g-s_i(f g)=(f-s_i(f))g+s_i(f)(g-s_i(g))$, including inverse generators by applying that rule to $f f^{-1}=1$. Moving a polynomial across a $T$ reduces the number of misplaced polynomial factors, and correction terms reduce the number of $T$ factors; the finite Hecke relations then span the remaining words by $T_w$. Thus $H_n^{\mathrm{aff}}$ is spanned over $P$ by the $T_w$, and the presentation anti-involution fixing $X_i,T_i$ gives right ordered spanning too.

A representation of the unlocalized presentation. Form $K\rtimes S_n$ with multiplication $(f\sigma)(g\tau)=f\sigma(g)\sigma\tau$. For distinct indices set $c_{ij}=(z-1)X_j/(X_j-X_i)$ and $d_{ij}=(X_j-zX_i)/(X_j-X_i)=z-c_{ij}$, and assign $T_i\mapsto c_{i,i+1}+d_{i,i+1}s_i$, $X_j\mapsto X_j$. The rational identities $c_{ij}+c_{ji}=z-1$ and $d_{ij}d_{ji}=z+(z-1)c_{ij}-c_{ij}^2$ give the quadratic relation. For three distinct indices, expansion of the two braid products in their six permutation coefficients agrees: the longest coefficients are $d_{ij}d_{ik}d_{jk}$ in either order; the two length-two coefficients agree by commuting scalar factors; the length-one and identity coefficients agree using $c_{ij}c_{jk}=c_{ik}(c_{ij}+c_{jk}-(z-1))$ together with the preceding quadratic identities. These identities follow by multiplying by the common product of the differences and expanding the polynomial numerators. Distant relations follow from disjoint variable pairs. Finally $T_if-s_i(f)T_i=c_{i,i+1}(f-s_i(f))$, so the Bernstein and mixed relations hold. All denominators here are nonzero polynomials in independent variables in the domain $P$. This defines a homomorphism from the unlocalized presented algebra to $K\rtimes S_n$.

Independence over the base ring. For a reduced word $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$, the coefficient of the group element $w$ in the image of $T_w$ is
$$D_w=d_{i_1,i_1+1}\,s_{i_1}(d_{i_2,i_2+1})\cdots(s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_{k-1}})(d_{i_k,i_k+1})\ne0.$$
Every factor is a nonzero rational function; every other term uses a proper subword and therefore represents a permutation of length less than $k$ by [F3]. In a finite relation $\sum_w f_wT_w=0$ with $f_w\in P$, select a label $w$ of maximal length with $f_w\ne0$. Its group-element coefficient is $f_wD_w$ and receives no contribution from any other label of that maximal length or from shorter labels, so it is nonzero in $K$, a contradiction. Hence the $T_w$ are $P$-linearly independent and the representation is injective. Since the Laurent monomials $X^a$ are an $R$-basis of $P$, this proves that $X^aT_w$ are an $R$-basis; the anti-involution proves the right basis. Tensoring this free basis with any commutative $R$-algebra preserves it, and tensoring the generators-and-relations presentation gives exactly the same affine presentation over that algebra. As the unused $U$ parameters do not enter the relations, any commutative coefficient ring with unit $z$ is obtained by sending every $U_a$ to $1$. Thus the asserted arbitrary base change is valid, without inverting differences in the base-changed algebra.

Localization and intertwiners. Let $S$ be the multiplicative set generated by all $X_i-X_j$ with $i\ne j$. It is invariant under $S_n$. The mixed formula of step 1.1 extends to $S^{-1}P$ by the same product rule and by solving the formula for inverses of elements of $S$; the correction remains in $S^{-1}P$. Consequently adjoining these inverses gives the algebra with free left coefficient module $\bigoplus_w(S^{-1}P)T_w$ and the same multiplication rules. This realizes the localization: the inverse formulas make it universal among homomorphisms inverting $S$, and its injective representation in $K\rtimes S_n$ follows from the identical maximal-length argument of step 1.3. In it put $\Phi_i=T_i-c_{i,i+1}$; the mixed formula gives $\Phi_if=s_i(f)\Phi_i$ for all $f\in S^{-1}P$. Products $\Phi_w$ along reduced words have unitriangular expansions in the $T_v$, because selecting every $T$ gives $T_w$ and selecting any scalar correction leaves strictly shorter words; thus they too form a basis over $S^{-1}P$. No parameter difference $U_a-U_b$, quantum factorial or Gram determinant is inverted.

Polynomial multiplication is injective over the universal domain. If $0\ne f\in P$ and $h=\sum_w f_wT_w$, then $fh=0$ gives $ff_w=0$ for each $w$ by step 1.3. Since $P$ is a domain, every $f_w=0$, so $h=0$. The right-basis argument gives the analogous right multiplication result. This injectivity assertion is over the universal domain, as in Statement (2), and does not assert injectivity of nonzero zero divisors after arbitrary base change.

Subword support in the localization. Expanding a reduced product $T_w=\prod_t(\Phi_{i_t}+c_{i_t,i_t+1})$ and moving coefficients left using step 2.1 gives terms supported on products of subwords of the reduced word. Every coefficient is a sum of products of permuted $c$ functions and hence has only variable-difference denominators. Equivalently, in the crossed product $\Phi_i=d_{i,i+1}s_i$, so moving a localized polynomial $f$ through such a term replaces it by the corresponding subword permutation applied to $f$. This proves the subword expansion used by consumers and the asserted intertwining throughout the embedded localization.

Conclusion. Step 1.3 proves both ordered bases over $R$ and after arbitrary base change with unit $z$; step 2.2 proves the universal-domain injectivity; and steps 2.1 and 3.1 prove the localized embedding and intertwining identity. For $n=0$ there are no polynomial or Hecke generators, $S_0$ consists of the identity, the lone ordered monomial is $1$, and $H_0^{\mathrm{aff}}=R$; all localization and intertwining clauses are then vacuous. No cyclotomic basis, trace form, primitive-content assertion or Brundan–Kleshchev result is used.

citations.quote:
Let $A$ be a commutative ring and let $z\in A$ be a unit. Fix an integer
$n\ge0$.

**The nondegenerate affine presentation.** The algebra
$H_n^{\mathrm{aff}}(A;z)$ is the $A$-algebra presented by commuting units
$X_1,\dots,X_n$ and generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]],
[[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]) subject to
$$T_r^2=(z-1)T_r+z,\qquad T_rT_{r+1}T_r=T_{r+1}T_rT_{r+1},\qquad T_rT_s=T_sT_r\quad(|r-s|>1),$$
$$T_rX_rT_r=zX_{r+1},\qquad T_rX_s=X_sT_r\quad(s\notin\{r,r+1\}),$$
the last two relations being the Bernstein relation and the distant mixed
commutation, and with $T_r$ invertible as a consequence of its quadratic
relation. For $n=0$ the algebra is $A$.

**The degenerate affine presentation.** The algebra
$H_n^{\deg}(A)$ is the $A$-algebra presented by commuting generators
$x_1,\dots,x_n$ and symmetric-group generators $s_1,\dots,s_{n-1}$ subject to
the Coxeter relations $s_r^2=1$, $s_rs_{r+1}s_r=s_{r+1}s_rs_{r+1}$,
$s_rs_t=s_ts_r$ for $|r-t|>1$ together with the mixed relations
$$s_rx_r=x_{r+1}s_r-1,\qquad s_rx_{r+1}=x_rs_r+1,\qquad s_rx_t=x_ts_r\quad(t\notin\{r,r+1\}).$$

**Auxiliary cyclotomic quotients.** For a monic polynomial
$f(u)=u^{\ell}+a_{\ell-1}u^{\ell-1}+\dots+a_0$ in $A[u]$ of degree $\ell$
impose the single relation $f(X_1)=0$ (respectively $f(x_1)=0$) on the FIRST
polynomial generator and call the resulting quotient the **monic cyclotomic
quotient**; when $\ell=0$, so that $f=1$, the quotient at positive rank is the
zero algebra, while rank zero remains $A$. In the nondegenerate case the
constant term $a_0$ is required to be a unit. The first-strand convention
imposed here (cyclotomic relation on $X_1$, and later induction appending on
the right) is the one used on this page.

**The charged cyclic specialization.** Let $A=F$ be a field, let
$z=q_H\in F^{\times}$ have finite quantum characteristic $e\ge2$
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]), and let
$I=\mathbb Z/e\mathbb Z$ be the cyclic **label set** of residues, with a
dominant cyclic type-A weight $(\lambda_i)_{i\in I}$, $\lambda_i\ge0$, and
$\ell=\sum_i\lambda_i$
([[def-cyclic-affine-type-a-cartan-datum]]). If $q_H\ne1$ use the
nondegenerate presentation and put $c_i:=q_H^{\,i}$; if $q_H=1$ (which forces
$\operatorname{char}F=e$) use the degenerate presentation and put
$c_i:=i\cdot1_F$. Impose
$$f(z_1)=\prod_{i\in I}(z_1-c_i)^{\lambda_i}$$
on the first generator ($z_1=X_1$ in the nondegenerate branch and $z_1=x_1$ in
the degenerate branch) and write $H_d^\Lambda$ for the resulting **charged
cyclotomic quotient** of rank $d$. This charged finite-$e$ branch is the scope
of the present page; the arbitrary-base affine and monic definitions above
supply its universal PBW and trace proof inputs. The definition itself asserts
no basis, no spectrum, no primitive block decomposition and no
Brundan–Kleshchev isomorphism. The grading variable $v$ of the KLR side is
independent of $q_H$.

**Well-definedness notes.** The nondegenerate parameters $c_i=q_H^i$ are
distinct because $q_H$ has multiplicative order exactly $e$; the degenerate
parameters $c_i=i\cdot1_F$ are distinct because $\operatorname{char}F=e$ makes
$i\cdot1_F\ne j\cdot1_F$ for $0\le i<j<e$. In the nondegenerate branch no
embedding of the label set $\mathbb Z/e\mathbb Z$ into $F$ is claimed or used:
$i$ is only a label for the value $q_H^i$. All these definitions are given by
generators, relations and a two-sided quotient ideal and use no choice
principle.

Let $n\ge0$ be an integer, with $S_0=\{1\}$ as in
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]. Let $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the ring of Laurent polynomials in one
indeterminate $v$ over $\mathbb Z$. For $n\ge2$ the **generic type-A Hecke
algebra** $H_v(n)$ is the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ and the relations
$$T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2),\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(1\le i,j<n,\ |i-j|>1),$$
that is, the quotient of the free unital associative $A$-algebra on
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ by the two-sided ideal generated by these relators. The
first relation is written in the **RG-13 quadratic normalization**
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, equivalent to the displayed form over $A$. For $n\le1$ there
are no generators and we set $H_v(n):=A$.

**Standard basis elements.** Let $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ with
simple transpositions $s_i=(i\ i+1)$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), and let $w\in S_n$ have inversion length $\ell(w)=\ell$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). Choose a reduced expression
$w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$, that is, a word of the minimal length $\ell(w)$
representing $w$, and put
$$T_w:=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}\in H_v(n),$$
the empty product when $w$ is the identity of $S_n$, so that $T_w=1$ for that
element. That $T_w$ is independent of the chosen reduced expression, and that
the elements $T_w$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, is proved in the
standard-basis theorem below
([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); the notation
distinguishes the generator $T_i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$ from $T_w$ for the group
element $w$.

**Specializations.** Let $R$ be a commutative $A$-algebra with structure map
$\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto v_0$, and suppose $v_0\in R^\times$. The
**specialization** of $H_v(n)$ at $v_0$ is the $R$-algebra
$R\otimes_AH_v(n)$; it is presented over $R$ by the images of $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$
subject to the same relations with $v$ replaced by $v_0$, and we write $H_{v_0}(n)$
for it. Two specializations are used on this page: $v\mapsto1$, where the
quadratic relation becomes $T_i^2=1$ together with the braid and commutation
relations, and $v\mapsto q$, where $q$ is the prime power defining
$\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$; the latter specializes the generic algebra to
the Hecke algebra attached to the finite general linear group. The condition
$v_0\in R^\times$ is part of the definition of a specialization and, for a nonzero coefficient ring $R$, excludes $v_0=0$. The zero ring
is allowed: its unique element is a unit and its specialization is the zero algebra.

In the generic type-A Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with
generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, the quadratic relations
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations, and with
$T_w$ the product of the $T_i$ along a reduced word for $w\in S_n$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]):

1. $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$; in particular $H_v(n)$ is
free of rank $n!$ over $A$;
2. for every $w\in S_n$ and every $1\le i\le n-1$,
$$T_wT_i=T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad T_wT_i=(v-1)T_w+v\,T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1,$$
where $\ell$ is the inversion length of $S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]); consequently the rule rewrites
every monomial in the generators as an $A$-linear combination of the $T_w$.

No choice principle is used.

For $n\ge2$, the symmetric group $S_n$ has the presentation

$$S_n=\langle s_1,\dots,s_{n-1}\mid s_i^2=1,\ s_is_{i+1}s_i=s_{i+1}s_is_{i+1},\ s_is_j=s_js_i\ (|i-j|>1)\rangle,$$

where, after relabelling the underlying set $n=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ as
$\{1,\ldots,n\}$, $s_i$ corresponds to the adjacent transposition
$(i\ i+1)$. For
$n=0,1$, the trivial group has the empty presentation.

derivations.claim: Elementary straightening of polynomials past a simple generator. In the nondegenerate branch the mixed relation gives, for a polynomial $p$ in the commuting variables, $T_rp=(s_rp)T_r-(q_H-1)X_{r+1}\frac{p-s_rp}{X_r-X_{r+1}},$ and in the degenerate branch $s_rp=(s_rp)s_r-\frac{p-s_rp}{x_r-x_{r+1}} .$ Both divided differences are polynomials: for $p=X_r^m$ the first identity is $T_rX_r^m=X_{r+1}^mT_r-(q_H-1)(X_r^{m-1}+X_r^{m-2}X_{r+1}+\dots+X_{r+1}^{m-1})X_{r+1}$, which follows from [F1] by induction on $m$, and the second is $s_rx_r^m=x_{r+1}^ms_r-\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}x_r^kx_{r+1}^{m-1-k}$, again by induction; the general case follows from the divided-difference product rule for the two variable replacements $X_r\leftrightarrow X_{r+1}$ and $x_r\leftrightarrow x_{r+1}$. Consequently any word in the generators and polynomial variables rewrites as an $A$-linear combination of ordered monomials $X^aT_w$ in the nondegenerate branch (the $T$-word reduced by [F2], polynomial factors collected by commutation) and of $x^aw$ in the degenerate branch. The nondegenerate straightening preserves total polynomial degree; the degenerate one lowers degree by one in the correction term.

The nondegenerate quotient is generated by positive powers. In the nondegenerate branch the relation $f(X_1)=0$ has nonzero constant term $a_0$, so $X_1^{-1}=-a_0^{-1}(X_1^{\ell-1}+a_{\ell-1}X_1^{\ell-2}+\dots+a_1)$ is a polynomial in $X_1$; and from $T_rX_rT_r=q_HX_{r+1}$ one gets $X_{r+1}^{-1}=q_HT_r^{-1}X_r^{-1}T_r^{-1}$ by inverting the equation. Starting from the displayed polynomial expression for $X_1^{-1}$ and iterating this forward recursion expresses every $X_r^{-1}$ through positive powers of $X_1$ and the $T$'s, since $T_r^{-1}=q_H^{-1}(T_r-q_H+1)$ is a polynomial in $T_r$. Therefore the quotient is already generated, as an $A$-module, by words in $X_1,\dots,X_d$ and the $T_r$, and step 1.1 applies to them.

The transported relations in the nondegenerate branch. Put $R_1:=f(X_1)$ and $R_{r+1}:=T_rR_rT_r$; each $R_r$ is zero in the quotient. We claim by induction on $r$ that ordered straightening writes $R_r=q_H^{r-1}X_r^{\ell}+\sum_{a,w}c_{a,w}X_1^{a_1}\cdots X_r^{a_r}T_w,$ where $w\in S_r$, $\sum_ja_j\le\ell$, $a_r<\ell$, and no variable of index above $r$ occurs. The case $r=1$ is the definition, with constant coefficient rearranged. For the induction step, direct summation of the mixed relation gives, for $m\ge1$, $T_rX_r^mT_r=q_HX_{r+1}^m-(q_H-1)\sum_{k=1}^{m-1}X_r^kX_{r+1}^{m-k}T_r,$ and for $m=0$ one uses $T_r^2=(q_H-1)T_r+q_H$. Transporting the leading term $q_H^{r-1}X_r^{\ell}$ therefore produces exactly $q_H^rX_{r+1}^{\ell}$ plus terms of $X_{r+1}$-degree below $\ell$. Each remainder monomial has $X_r$-degree $a_r<\ell$; variables of index below $r$ commute with $T_r$ and with $X_{r+1}$, and $T_w\in H_r$ for $w\in S_r$, so applying the displayed formula to $X_r^{a_r}$ and then straightening the finite words $T_rT_wT_r$, $T_wT_r$ by [F2] produces terms of $X_{r+1}$-degree at most $a_r<\ell$ and total polynomial degree at most $\ell$. This proves the claim.

The transported relations in the degenerate branch. Put $R_1:=f(x_1)$ and $R_{r+1}:=s_rR_rs_r$. Straightening and induction on $r$ show $R_r=x_r^{\ell}+\sum_{a,w}c_{a,w}x^aw,$ where $w\in S_r$, all occurring variables have index at most $r$, and $\sum_ja_j<\ell$: conjugation transports $x_r^m$ by $s_rx_r^ms_r=x_{r+1}^m-\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}x_r^kx_{r+1}^{m-1-k}s_r,$ so the leading term $x_r^{\ell}$ produces $x_{r+1}^{\ell}$ plus correction terms of total degree $\ell-1$, and every old remainder, when straightened, stays of degree below $\ell$.

Termination of the nondegenerate reduction. Order exponent vectors lexicographically as $(a_d,a_{d-1},\dots,a_1)$, larger first differing coordinate larger; this is a well-order on $\mathbb N^d$ preserved by addition. Suppose $a_r\ge\ell$ for some $r$ and some spanning monomial $X^aT_w$. Multiplying the zero relation $R_r$ of step 2.2 on the left by $X^{a-\ell e_r}$ and on the right by $T_w$ gives a relation whose leading term is $q_H^{r-1}X^aT_w$ and whose remaining terms all have the same coordinates above $r$ and a strictly smaller $r$-th coordinate (increases in coordinates below $r$ do not affect the lexicographic comparison), with $w\in S_r$ and finite straightening changing no dot exponents. Since $q_H^{r-1}$ is a unit, this solves for $X^aT_w$ as a combination of spanning monomials with strictly smaller exponent vector; well-founded induction on the lexicographic order terminates and expresses every element using only monomials with every $a_r<\ell$. Hence the bounded ordered monomials span the nondegenerate quotient, over $A$ and after any base change.

Termination of the degenerate reduction. If $a_r\ge\ell$, multiply the zero relation $R_r$ of step 2.3 on the left by $x^{a-\ell e_r}$ and on the right by $w$; the leading term is $x^aw$, and every other term has total degree strictly below $\sum_ja_j$ (all other coefficients come from the remainder of $R_r$, of degree $<\ell$). Induction on the total degree $\sum_ja_j$ therefore expresses every element in terms of monomials $x^aw$ with all $a_r<\ell$. This also shows that no relation $f(x_r)=0$ for $r>1$ is claimed: at level one $f(t)=t$, and $x_1=0$ gives $x_2=s_1$, which is exactly the form of the reduced spanning family.

Conclusion. Steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1 give the spanning statement for the nondegenerate quotient by $f(X_1)=0$, and steps 1.1, 2.3 and 3.2 for the degenerate quotient by $f(x_1)=0$, with all exponents $a_r<\ell$ in both branches and no independence asserted. Since the spanning families have at most $\ell^dd!$ elements, each quotient has dimension at most $\ell^dd!$ over a field. The specialisations $f(t)=\prod_i(t-q_H^i)^{\lambda_i}$ and $f(t)=\prod_i(t-i)^{\lambda_i}$ are instances of the two branches with $\ell=\sum_i\lambda_i$. For $\ell=0$ the imposed relation is $1=0$, giving the zero algebra for $d>0$ and $A$ for $d=0$, as stated.

derivations.claim: The operator model. Let $S_r$ be the automorphism of $K$ swapping $z_r,z_{r+1}$ and fixing the other variables, and put $\delta_r:=z_r-z_{r+1}$. Let $z_j$ act on $K$ by multiplication and let $A_r:=S_r+\frac{S_r-1}{\delta_r}=\Bigl(1+\frac1{\delta_r}\Bigr)S_r-\frac1{\delta_r}.$ For $p\in P$ the difference $S_rp-p$ is divisible by $\delta_r$ in $P$ (write $p$ in the variables $z_r,z_{r+1}$ with the remaining variables as scalars and use that $z_r^az_{r+1}^b-z_{r+1}^az_r^b$ is divisible by $\delta_r$), so $A_r$ preserves $P$; hence the operators $z_j$ (multiplication) and $A_r$ generate a subalgebra of $\operatorname{End}_F(K)$ and, restricted to $P$, of $\operatorname{End}_F(P)$. [given, construct]

Verification of the defining relations in the model. Direct substitution gives the mixed relations $A_rz_r-z_{r+1}A_r=-1$, $A_rz_{r+1}-z_rA_r=1$, and $A_rz_j=z_jA_r$ for $j\notin\{r,r+1\}$. Writing $a(t):=1+1/t$ and $b(t):=-1/t$, so that $A_r=a(\delta_r)S_r+b(\delta_r)$, and using $S_r(\delta_r)=-\delta_r$, the identity coefficient of $A_r^2$ is $a(\delta_r)a(-\delta_r)+b(\delta_r)^2=1$ and its $S_r$-coefficient is $a(\delta_r)b(-\delta_r)+b(\delta_r)a(\delta_r)=0$, so $A_r^2=1$; distant $A_r$ commute because their permutations and coefficients involve disjoint variable pairs. For the braid relation put $u:=z_r-z_{r+1}$, $v:=z_{r+1}-z_{r+2}$, $w:=u+v=z_r-z_{r+2}$, $S:=S_r$, $T:=S_{r+1}$; expanding $A_rA_{r+1}A_r$ and $A_{r+1}A_rA_{r+1}$ in $K\rtimes S_d$ gives the six permutation coefficients $-\frac{uv+1}{uvw}\ (1),\quad \frac{a(u)}{vw}\ (S),\quad \frac{a(v)}{uw}\ (T),\quad -\frac{a(u)a(w)}{v}\ (ST),\quad -\frac{a(v)a(w)}{u}\ (TS),\quad a(u)a(w)a(v)\ (STS),$ and the right expansion has the same six coefficients with $u,v$ and $S,T$ interchanged, so the two expansions agree. These are rational identities valid in every characteristic, including $2$. Hence the assignment $z_j\mapsto$ multiplication by $z_j$, $s_r\mapsto A_r$ defines an algebra homomorphism $H_d^{\deg}\to\operatorname{End}_F(K)$ (and into $\operatorname{End}_F(P)$ by step 1.1). [F1, algebra]

Spanning. In the model, $s_rp=(S_rp)s_r-(p-S_rp)\delta_r^{-1}$ for every polynomial $p$, so every word in the generators rewrites as a linear combination of the ordered monomials $z^aw$ with $a_j\ge0$ and $w\in S_d$, the power-polynomial part being collected by commutativity and the $s$-word reduced by [F2]. The same straightening performed in $H_d^{\deg}$ (available there because the model satisfies the defining relations, or by the same elementary computation in the presentation) shows that the ordered monomials span the algebra. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

Conclusion. Steps 3.1 and 2.1 show that the family $\{x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_d^{a_d}w:a_j\ge0,\ w\in S_d\}$ both spans and is linearly independent in $H_d^{\deg}$ over $F$; renaming the commuting generators $z_j\mapsto x_j$ and using the presentation [F1] gives the asserted $F$-basis. No cyclotomic quotient, BK isomorphism or dimension theorem is used, and for $d=0$ the family consists of the empty monomial alone. [step 3.1, step 3.2] ∎

Every idempotent $e$ in a finite-dimensional unital $k$-algebra $A$ is a finite sum of pairwise orthogonal primitive idempotents of $A$. Here primitive means nonzero and admitting no decomposition as two nonzero orthogonal idempotents; zero is the empty sum.

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra and $M$ a finite-dimensional left $A$-module. Then $M$ has a projective cover. If $\pi:P\to M$ and $\rho:Q\to M$ are projective covers, then there is an isomorphism $f:P\to Q$ with $\rho\circ f=\pi$.
Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra over a field and let $J=J(A)$. Then $J$ is nilpotent, and the quotient algebra $A/J$ is semisimple.
Any two composition series of a module have the same length, and their simple factors agree up to permutation and isomorphism.

A **composition series** of a left $R$-module $M$ is a finite chain $$0=M_0<M_1<\cdots<M_n=M$$ whose factors $M_i/M_{i-1}$ are simple. If such a series exists, the **length** $\ell_R(M)$ is its number $n$ of factors; [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]] proves independence of the chosen series.

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital $F$-algebra with centre $Z(A):=\{z\in A:za=az\text{ for all }a\in A\}$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). A **central idempotent** of $A$ is an idempotent $e\in Z(A)$; it is **primitive** when $e\ne0$ and $e$ is not the sum of two nonzero orthogonal central idempotents.

derivations.claim: The cell-form scalar and its symmetry. For basis elements $c^\lambda_{us},c^\lambda_{tv}$ the product $c^\lambda_{us}c^\lambda_{tv}$ equals a scalar $G_\lambda(s,t)$ times $c^\lambda_{uv}$ modulo $A^{>\lambda}$ with $G_\lambda(s,t)$ independent of $u,v$: the right cell axiom fixes the first index and the left cell axiom fixes the last one, and comparing the two evaluations leaves the same scalar. The cellular involution gives $G_\lambda(s,t)=G_\lambda(t,s)$. Associativity of the threefold product yields $\langle xa,y\rangle=\langle x,ya^*\rangle$, since both sides compute the coefficient in the cell layer of the same product.

Cell purity and the zero cell. If $T(\lambda)$ is empty, then $C_\lambda=0$, its Gram matrix and form quotient are zero, and every central block projection acts with zero image; thus its block support is empty and it has no simple factors. The corresponding cell layer $J_\lambda$ is zero as well. Now assume $C_\lambda\ne0$ and let $z$ be a central idempotent of $A$. On the cell layer $J_\lambda\cong C_\lambda^*\otimes_FC_\lambda$ the equality of left and right multiplication by $z$ gives $B\otimes\operatorname{Id}=\operatorname{Id}\otimes A_\lambda$ for the first- and second-factor coefficient matrices; comparing matrix coefficients shows every off-diagonal entry of $B$ and $A_\lambda$ vanishes and all diagonal entries of $B$ and $A_\lambda$ are equal, so both are a single scalar $\theta_\lambda$ times the identity. Since $z$ is idempotent, $\theta_\lambda\in\{0,1\}$. Applying this to all primitive central idempotents, whose sum is $1$, exactly one acts as $1$ on the nonzero cell module $C_\lambda$ and the others as $0$; hence $C_\lambda$, and therefore every composition factor of it, lies in one block. This covers labels with zero-form quotient because the tensor argument never divides by the Gram matrix.

Nonzero form gives a simple head. Let $R_\lambda:=\{x\in C_\lambda:\langle x,C_\lambda\rangle=0\}$ be the radical of the form. By step 1.1 the rank-one action is $xc^\lambda_{uv}=\langle x,c^\lambda_u\rangle c^\lambda_v$, which shows that $R_\lambda$ is a submodule and that every vector $x\notin R_\lambda$ generates $C_\lambda$: if $\langle x,c^\lambda_u\rangle\ne0$, then scaling $xc^\lambda_{uv}$ by the inverse scalar produces $c^\lambda_v$ for every $v$. Hence every proper submodule is contained in $R_\lambda$ and $D_\lambda=C_\lambda/R_\lambda$ is simple when the form is nonzero; the criterion is nonzero form, and a degenerate but nonzero form is allowed. Extending scalars preserves the Gram rank and the rank-one action, so $D_\lambda$ is absolutely simple.

Every simple occurs. Let $D$ be a simple $A$-module, and choose a cell ideal $I_\lambda$ acting nontrivially on $D$, maximal among such ideals in the finite cell order; then $A^{>\lambda}$ annihilates $D$, while $J_\lambda=I_\lambda/A^{>\lambda}$ does not, so $DJ_\lambda=D$. If the Gram matrix of $C_\lambda$ were zero, the cell-layer multiplication would satisfy $J_\lambda^2=0$ and $DJ_\lambda^2=0$, a contradiction; hence the form is nonzero. Choose $s,u$ and $d\in D$ with $dc^\lambda_{su}\ne0$; the map $c^\lambda_v\mapsto dc^\lambda_{sv}$ has nonzero image, which is all of $D$ by simplicity and factors through the nonzero head $D_\lambda$ of step 2.1, so $D\cong D_\lambda$. This exhausts the simple labels without classifying which multipartitions have nonzero forms.

Since $D_\mu$ does not annihilate $I_\mu$ by the rank-one action, $[C_\lambda:D_\mu]\ne0$ forces $\lambda\ge\mu$. Blocks and linkage. A finite split algebra has blocks equal to the connected components of the graph on its primitive idempotents with an edge $e$–$f$ whenever $eAf\ne0$ or $fAe\ne0$: a sum of full primitive idempotents over a union of components is central, and conversely a central idempotent cannot separate a nonzero corner, while repeated primitive idempotents of the same simple are linked through the matrix units of $A/\operatorname{rad}A$. By step 4.1 two simple labels have a nonzero corner exactly when they occur together as factors of some cell module, so two simples share a block exactly when a chain of cell modules links their factors. Since by step 1.2 every nonzero cell module is pure and by step 3.1 every simple occurs in a nonzero-form head, two nonzero cell modules lie in the same block exactly when there is a finite chain of nonzero cell modules each neighbouring pair of which shares a simple composition factor. Each nonzero cell has a simple composition factor because it has positive finite dimension. A zero cell has no such factor and has empty block support by step 1.2, so it is absent from this support graph and cannot create a chain edge or a common supported block.

Conclusion. Steps 1.1, 2.1, 3.1 and 3.2 prove the head, exhaustion, order and multiplicity statement (1); step 1.2 proves cell purity (2); step 4.1 proves the corner identity (4); and step 5.1 proves the exact shared-factor linkage criterion (3). All arguments work over every field and allow degenerate nonzero cell forms, nonzero cells with zero-form quotient, and empty index sets with zero cell modules and empty block support.

Let $O$ be a discrete valuation ring with uniformizer $\pi$ and residue field
$F=O/\pi O$ ([[def-discrete-valuation-ring]]), and let $\nu_\pi$ denote its
valuation. Let $M$ be a finite free $O$-module with an $O$-valued bilinear
pairing $b$ ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]) whose scalar extension to
$\operatorname{Frac}(O)$ is nondegenerate. For $s\ge0$ put
$$M(s):=\{x\in M:b(x,M)\subseteq\pi^sO\},\qquad M_F^s:=(M(s)+\pi M)/\pi M .$$
Then:

1. $M_F^0=M/\pi M$ and $M_F^1=\operatorname{rad}(b_F)$, where $b_F$ is the
   reduced pairing on $M_F$;
2. the filtration terminates ($M_F^s=0$ for all sufficiently large $s$), and
   for any Gram matrix $G$ of $b$ one has the exact identity
   $$\sum_{s>0}\dim_FM_F^s=\nu_\pi(\det G);$$
3. if an $O$-algebra $A$ acts on $M$ with an anti-involution $*$ satisfying
   $b(ax,y)=b(x,a^*y)$ for all $a\in A$, $x,y\in M$, then every $M(s)$, and
   hence every $M_F^s$, is an $A$-submodule;
4. if $M_F$ is a cellular standard module with nonzero cellular form
   ([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]), then
   $\operatorname{rad}(b_F)$ is its unique maximal submodule and therefore
   coincides with its module radical
   ([[def-module-radical-socle-head-and-loewy-series]]).

The Smith reduction used in the proof works over $O$ without any
characteristic restriction, in particular in characteristic $2$; it uses
independent bases of $M$ and of $M^*=\operatorname{Hom}_O(M,O)$, never a
diagonalization of a symmetric form.

Let $R$ be a ring. A **left $R$-module** is an abelian group $(M,+,0_M)$ with a
scalar action $R\times M\to M$, $(r,m)\mapsto rm$, satisfying

$$r(m+n)=rm+rn,\quad (r+s)m=rm+sm,\quad (rs)m=r(sm),\quad 1_Rm=m.$$

A **right $R$-module** has an action $M\times R\to M$, $(m,r)\mapsto mr$, with
the analogous right-handed axioms. Unless “right” is stated, **module** means a
unital left module.

Let $\mathcal C$ be an essentially small abelian category
([[def-abelian-category]]). Its set of isomorphism classes is denoted
$\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal C)$. The **Grothendieck group** of $\mathcal C$ is

$$ G_0(\mathcal C):=\mathbb Z[\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal C)]\big/\langle e_Y-e_X-e_Z:\ 0\to X\to Y\to Z\to 0\text{ is short exact in }\mathcal C\rangle. $$

where $\mathbb Z[\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal C)]$ is the free abelian group on
that set ([[def-free-abelian-group]]) and $[X]$ denotes the image of the
generator for the isomorphism class of $X$. Thus the defining relation is
$[Y]=[X]+[Z]$ for every short exact sequence
([[def-exact-sequence-and-short-exact-sequence-in-an-abelian-category]]).
This is the short-exact-sequence group, distinguished below from split
Grothendieck groups of projectives. No free abelian group on the possibly
class-sized collection of all objects is formed. The sequence
$0\to0\to0\to0$ in particular gives $[0]=0$.

citations.quote: Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]). A function $a\colon\mathbb N\to R$ has **finite support** when there is $N\in\mathbb N$ such that $a_i=0$ for every $i>N$. The **polynomial ring** $R[x]$ is the set of all finitely supported functions $a\colon\mathbb N\to R$. For $a,b\in R[x]$ and $n\in\mathbb N$, define $$ (a+b)_n:=a_n+b_n,\qquad (ab)_n:=\sum_{i+j=n}a_i b_j.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ be the iterated polynomial ring. Every permutation $\sigma\in\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\ldots,n\})$ acts on it by $$\sigma\cdot f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=f(x_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,x_{\sigma(n)}).$$ A polynomial $f\in R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ is **symmetric** when $\sigma\cdot f=f$ for every permutation $\sigma$.

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital $F$-algebra with centre $Z(A):=\{z\in A:za=az\text{ for all }a\in A\}$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). A **central idempotent** of $A$ is an idempotent $e\in Z(A)$; it is **primitive** when $e\ne0$ and $e$ is not the sum of two nonzero orthogonal central idempotents.

derivations.claim: The nilpotent ideal of the content summand. For $1\le k\le d$ let $a_k$ be the value of $\sigma_k$ on any word of content $\alpha$ (independent of the order of the word). On the summand $p_{\mathrm{word}}A$ inside $eA$ write $x_r=\mathrm{word}_r+N_r$ with commuting nilpotents $N_r$ by [F1]. Choose $M$ with $N_r^M=0$ for all $r$; then every product of more than $d(M-1)$ monomials of positive degree in the $N_r$ vanishes, because among more than $d(M-1)$ factors some $N_r$ occurs at least $M$ times (finite pigeonhole). Hence every polynomial in the $N_r$ with zero constant term is nilpotent, and in particular $N_k:=e\sigma_k(x)-a_ke$ is nilpotent on every $p_{\mathrm{word}}A$; since there are finitely many words, a common exponent makes $N_k$ nilpotent in $eA$. The $N_k$ commute, and the ideal $J$ they generate in the commutative ring $eZ(A)$ is nilpotent by the same degree count. [F1, algebra]

The center of the content summand is a local ring. By [F2] every symmetric polynomial is a polynomial in $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_d$ (the characteristic-free lexicographic reduction), so the symmetric-center hypothesis gives $eZ(A)=Fe+J .$ Since $e\ne0$ and $J$ is nilpotent, $Fe\cap J=0$: a nonzero element of the intersection is a scalar multiple of $e$ lying in every power of $J$, hence is $0$. Therefore $eZ(A)/J\cong F$, a field, and by [F3] every idempotent of $eZ(A)$ is $0$ or $e$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

The nonzero content idempotents are exactly the primitive central idempotents. Step 2.1 shows that each $e_\alpha\ne0$ is a primitive idempotent of $Z(A)$, hence primitive central in $A$. Conversely, let $b$ be a primitive central idempotent of $A$. derivations.claim: Beta sets, bead moves and the rim-hook dictionary. By [F1] a bead move $u\mapsto u-h$ with $u\in B$, $u-h\notin B$ unwraps a rim hook of length $h$ whose foot has residue $u-h+1$ modulo $e$: if $\beta_i=u$ and $\beta_j<u-h<\beta_{j-1}$, the rows $i,\dots,j-1$ change by the boundary between those two beta positions, the lost border strip has $h$ boxes, and its lowest-row leftmost lost column makes the foot content $u-h+1$; reversing the move wraps a hook with foot residue the starting beta position plus one. Moving a bead one position upward on its runner therefore removes an $e$-hook, and packing every runner upward leaves the number of beads relative to the negative reference tail on each runner unchanged; by [F2] the result is the componentwise $e$-core independent of the order. Every $e$-hook contains one node of each residue, so hook removal preserves the hub (the residue-count vector modulo the all-one vector) and subtracts the all-one vector from the residue counts. [F1, F2, algebra]

The boundary-count identity. Let $C_i$ be the residue counts and $\delta_i$ the number of removable minus addable $i$-nodes. We prove $\delta_i=2C_i-C_{i-1}-C_{i+1}-m_i$ by induction while adjoining nodes to the empty multipartition. The empty multipartition has $C_i=0$ for all $i$ and $\delta_i=-m_i$ (each component contributes one addable first node of its residue $c_a$ in the empty diagram), which gives the identity initially. Adjoining a node of residue $j$ changes the boundary count by $+2$ at $j$ and $-1$ at each of $j-1$ and $j+1$ (counted twice when $e=2$); these changes are read off by recording the occupied and vacant beta positions before and after the corresponding one-position bead move, all other adjacent occupancies cancelling. The right-hand side changes in exactly the same way because $C_j$ increases by $1$ and $C_i$ for $i\ne j$ is unchanged. Induction on the number of nodes gives the identity for every multipartition. [F1, algebra]

Cores and their height matrices. For a componentwise $e$-core let $b_{ia}$ be the largest bead on runner $i$ ($0\le i<e$) and $t_{ia}=(b_{ia}-i)/e$, so the packed beta set on runner $i$ is $\{i+ek:k\le t_{ia}\}$. Counting beads $\ge-eL$ for large $L$ gives the column sums $\sum_i t_{ia}=c_a-e$. Writing $R_i=\sum_at_{ia}$, the hub satisfies $\delta_i=R_i-R_{i-1}$ for $1\le i<e$ and $\delta_0=R_0-R_{e-1}-\ell$; since $\sum_iR_i=\sum_ac_a-e\ell$ is fixed, equal hub is equivalent to equal row sums. Hence cores of a fixed hub and fixed charges are exactly the integer $e\times\ell$ matrices $T=(t_{ia})$ with fixed row sums $R_i$ and column sums $c_a-e$. [F1, F2, algebra]

Switches and energy. Let $T$ be an integer $e\times\ell$ matrix with fixed margins, and consider a switch in distinct rows $i,j$ and distinct columns $a,b$, replacing $(t_{ia},t_{ib},t_{ja},t_{jb})$ by $(t_{ia}-1,t_{ib}+1,t_{ja}+1,t_{jb}-1)$; margins are preserved. With $\gamma:=t_{ia}-t_{ib}-t_{ja}+t_{jb}$, the squared-norm changes by $4-2\gamma$: so $\gamma=2$ is a zero-energy switch and $\gamma\ge3$ strictly lowers the energy. Regard the $e$ labelled rows of $T$ as a multiset in $L_\ell=\mathbb Z^\ell/\mathbb Z(1,\dots,1)$; it is tight exactly when $\gamma\le2$ for all choices, and switches with $\gamma=2$ are exactly the zero exchanges of [F3]. [F3, algebra]

Equal hub and equal size give equal content. If two multipartitions have equal hubs, the difference $d_i$ of their residue counts satisfies $2d_i-d_{i-1}-d_{i+1}=0$ by step 1.2, because the $\delta_i$ and $m_i$ terms are unchanged; hence all first differences $d_i-d_{i-1}$ are equal, and summing them around the cycle makes this common difference $0$, so $d$ is constant. Therefore equal hub and equal size imply equal content, and equal hubs imply sizes congruent modulo $e$. [step 1.2, algebra]

The size formula. If $T(\kappa),T(\eta)$ are the height matrices of two such cores, then $|\eta|-|\kappa|=\frac e2\Bigl(\sum_{i,a}t_{ia}(\eta)^2-\sum_{i,a}t_{ia}(\kappa)^2\Bigr).$ Indeed, count the beta numbers $\ge-eL$ in a component: their number is $eL+c_a$, the same for both cores, while their sum changes by $\sum_i i\,\Delta t_{ia}+\frac e2\sum_i\Delta(t_{ia}^2+t_{ia})$; from $\beta_j=\lambda_j+c_a-j$ the change in that sum equals the change in the partition size, and summing over $a$ the equal row sums kill $\sum_i i\sum_a\Delta t_{ia}$ while the equal column sums kill the linear $\sum\Delta t_{ia}$ term. In particular the squared-norm difference is even, so the displayed size difference is an integer multiple of $e$. [F1, step 1.3, algebra]

Ultra-tight rows and the global minimum. If the row multiset is not ultra-tight, a finite sequence of zero switches leads to a non-tight matrix, at which some rows and columns have $\gamma\ge3$, giving a strict descent: every intermediate matrix has the same margins, zero switches preserve core size by step 2.2, and a strict descent lowers core size by $e(\gamma-2)\ge e$. If instead the multiset is ultra-tight, [F3] supplies a column potential $s_a$ with every row of $U=(t_{ia}-s_a)$ having maximum minus minimum at most one. For a fixed row sum such a row minimizes the sum of squares over all integer rows: if two entries differ by at least $2$, transferring one from the larger to the smaller lowers the square sum by at least $2$, and repeated transfers terminate; the minimum is attained exactly by rows whose entries differ by at most one. Column potentials do not affect comparisons of total squared norm between matrices with the same column sums, because $\sum_{i,a}(t_{ia}-s_a)^2=\sum_{i,a}t_{ia}^2-2\sum_as_a\sum_it_{ia}+e\sum_as_a^2 .$ Hence such a $T$ is a global minimum among the matrices of its margins, and conversely a global minimum admits no strict descent after zero switches, so its row multiset is ultra-tight. Starting from any $T$, repeated zero-path and strict-descent steps reach a global minimum, since all matrices represent genuine cores of nonnegative integer size and strict descent lowers that size by at least $e$; minima therefore exist for every nonempty fixed-hub class. [F3, step 1.3, step 2.2, step 1.4, algebra]

Equal-size connectivity of minima. Let $T,V$ be two global minima with the same margins, and let $s$ be the column potential of $T$ from step 3.1. Every row of $U=T-s$ is balanced, with entries $u_i$ or $u_i+1$; since $V-s$ has the same row sums and the same total energy, each of its rows also attains the row minimum and has entries $u_i$ or $u_i+1$. Subtracting $u_i$ from row $i$ produces two binary $e\times\ell$ matrices $A,B$ with identical row and column sums. If $A\ne B$, the difference $D=A-B$ has entries $0,\pm1$ and zero row and column sums; starting from a $+1$ and alternating a $-1$ in the same row with a $+1$ in the same column produces a shortest alternating cycle with distinct rows $i_0,\dots,i_{t-1}$ and columns $j_0,\dots,j_{t-1}$, where $D_{i_kj_k}=+1$ and $D_{i_kj_{k+1}}=-1$. If $t=2$, switch the rectangle in $A$ to agree with $B$ there. If $t>2$, inspect $A_{i_0j_{t-1}}$ and $B_{i_0j_{t-1}}$: if $A_{i_0j_{t-1}}=0$, switching the rectangle with rows $i_0,i_{t-1}$ and columns $j_0,j_{t-1}$ gives a binary $A'$ with strictly fewer discrepancies from $B$; if $B_{i_0j_{t-1}}=1$, the reverse switch on $B$ gives a binary $B'$ with strictly fewer discrepancies from $A$; if neither holds, $D_{i_0j_{t-1}}=+1$ and a shorter alternating cycle exists, contradicting minimality. Induction on the discrepancy count connects $A$ and $B$ by binary switches, all preserving margins. Lifting these binary switches back to $T$ gives switches with $\gamma=2$, hence equal core size by step 2.2, preserving the hub. [F3, step 3.1, algebra]

Conclusion. Step 1.2 proves the boundary-count identity $\delta_i=2C_i-C_{i-1}-C_{i+1}-m_i$ with the double edge at $e=2$, and step 2.1 shows that equal hub and equal size are equivalent to equal content. Steps 1.3 and 2.2 identify cores of fixed hub and charges with integer matrices of fixed margins and give the squared-norm size formula; step 3.1 provides a same-hub core-switch path that never increases size and strictly decreases it whenever the core is not of minimum size, with minima existing in every nonempty class; and step 4.1 connects any two minimum-size cores by equal-size switches. These are exactly the finite-$e$ descent and reduced-core connectivity facts consumed by the Lyle–Mathas max-weight argument, proved locally without importing weight nonnegativity or matrix-alignment inputs. [step 3.1, step 2.1, step 4.1] ∎

derivations.claim: Rank decomposition. For fixed $d$, the corner idempotents $e(\beta,i)$ over all root components $\beta$ of height $d-1$ and colors $i$ are orthogonal and sum to $1_{B_d}$: each word has exactly one last color and one prefix root, so it lies in exactly one corner. By [F1] the multiplication map $\bigoplus_{\beta,i}B_de(\beta,i)\otimes_{R^\Lambda(\beta)}R^\Lambda(\beta)\to B_d$ is an isomorphism; spelling out the left action by the basic induction functor gives $P_d=DP_{d-1}=D^dP_0$. The zero-corner case gives $B_de(\beta,i)=0$ and is included since its summand is zero. [F1, F3, algebra]

The mixed commutators at $v=1$. Forgetting the grading shifts in the same-color categorical decomposition gives $[E_i^{\mathrm{basic}},F_i^{\mathrm{basic}}]=h_i(\Lambda-\beta)\operatorname{Id}$ on the root component $\beta$; its positive identity summands contribute $h_i$ copies and its negative identity summands contribute the signed counterpart, so the integral $[h_i]_v$ specializes at $v=1$ to the integer $h_i$ with no division by $v-v^{-1}$. The unequal-color mixed relation gives $[E_i^{\mathrm{basic}},F_j^{\mathrm{basic}}]=0$ for $i\ne j$. Hence $[E,D]=\sum_i[E_i^{\mathrm{basic}},F_i^{\mathrm{basic}}] =\Bigl(\sum_ih_i(\Lambda-\beta)\Bigr)\operatorname{Id}$ on root component $\beta$. For affine type A every Cartan column sums to zero, including the double-edge matrix at $e=2$, so $\sum_ih_i(\Lambda-\beta)=\sum_i\lambda_i-\sum_j\beta_j\sum_ia_{ij}=\ell$ independently of $\beta$. Therefore $[E,D]=\ell\cdot\operatorname{Id}$, and since rank-zero restriction is zero, $EP_0=0$; expanding $[E,D^d]=d\ell D^{d-1}$ gives $EP_d=d\ell\,P_{d-1}$. [F2, algebra]

The Hom-norm recurrence. For finite graded projectives define $h$ as in [F4]; it is additive in both variables, unchanged by shifts, and descends to projective $K_0$ modulo $v-1$. Pairing distinct root blocks by zero and summing over a fixed rank, the ordinary first adjunction $F_i^{\mathrm{basic}}\dashv E_i^{\mathrm{basic}}$ gives $h(F_i^{\mathrm{basic}}P,Q)=h(P,E_i^{\mathrm{basic}}Q)$, hence $h(DP,Q)=h(P,EQ)$; all restricted modules remain finite projectives by [F3], so the recurrence stays inside the declared group. Combining with step 1.2, $h(P_d,P_d)=h(DP_{d-1},P_d)=h(P_{d-1},EP_d) =d\ell\,h(P_{d-1},P_{d-1}).$ [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

Conclusion. The initial value is $h(P_0,P_0)=\dim_F\operatorname{End}_F(F)=1$; since $\operatorname{End}_{B_d}(B_d)\cong B_d^{\mathrm{op}}$ by right multiplication, $h(P_d,P_d)=\dim_FB_d$, and induction on $d$ gives $\dim_FB_d=\ell^dd!$ as an ordinary integer. Nothing reduces the integer dimension or the factor $d\ell$ inside $F$, so the argument covers every field characteristic; for $\ell=0$ and $d>0$ the recurrence gives $\dim_FB_d=0$; and for $d=0$, independently of $\ell$, $B_0=F$ has the singleton empty monomial as basis. No Frobenius theorem, tensor-form perfectness, highest-weight or global-basis isometry, Hecke basis or choice principle is used. [step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎
